title: School Access to Emergency Epinephrine Act
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was introduced. The summary of that version is repeated here.)

School Access to Emergency Epinephrine Act - Amends the Public Health Service Act, with respect to asthma-related grants for child health services, to give an additional preference to a state that allows self-administration of asthma and anaphylaxis medication and makes a certification concerning the adequacy of the state's civil liability protection law to protect trained school personnel who may administer epinephrine to a student reasonably believed to be having an anaphylactic reaction.

Requires elementary and secondary schools in such a state to: (1) permit trained personnel to administer epinephrine to a student reasonably believed to be having such a reaction, (2) maintain a supply of epinephrine in a secure location that is easily accessible to trained personnel for such treatment, and (3) have in place a plan for having on the school premises during operating hours one or more designated personnel trained in administration of epinephrine.

summary.headline: A 2013 federal law gives states a funding preference if they let trained school staff give epinephrine to students having severe allergic reactions.
summary.what_it_does: The law changes a federal asthma-related grant program for child health services. States get extra consideration for these grants if they allow students to use asthma and allergy medicine on their own and certify that their civil liability law adequately protects trained school staff who give epinephrine. The law does not itself require schools to act; the requirements apply to schools in states that qualify for the preference. Those schools must allow trained staff to give epinephrine to a student reasonably believed to be having a severe allergic reaction, keep a supply in a secure but easy-to-reach place, and have trained staff available during school hours.

who_it_affects.group: State governments that apply for federal child health grants
who_it_affects.how: They can earn a funding preference by allowing student self-administration of asthma and anaphylaxis medication and certifying their liability protection for trained school staff.

who_it_affects.group: Elementary and secondary schools in states that qualify for the preference
who_it_affects.how: They must let trained personnel give epinephrine to students having a suspected anaphylactic reaction, keep a secure but accessible supply, and have trained designated staff on site during operating hours.

who_it_affects.group: School nurses and other trained school personnel
who_it_affects.how: They may be permitted to give epinephrine to a student in a suspected severe allergic reaction, with legal protection under the state's liability law.

who_it_affects.group: Students with severe allergies or asthma
who_it_affects.how: Their schools in qualifying states must have epinephrine available and trained staff on hand to respond to an anaphylactic reaction.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Enacted November 13, 2013; the summary does not specify a separate effective date or compliance deadline for the school requirements.
